newsitem.title: UK: Oil markets struggle with rising Iraq, OPEC supply.
newsitem.headline: Oil markets struggle with rising Iraq, OPEC supply.

text.p: World oil prices eased lower again on Thursday as the market struggled under the weight of rising supplies in what is traditionally a slack season for oil demand.

The return of Iraqi barrels, combined with increased production by members of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) in February has hit the oil market hard as it treads water between the winter heating oil and summer gasoline seasons.

"The full impact of this supply surge (of Iraqi oil) will be felt heavily this spring, and will continue to weigh down prices," said an oil market report by Washington-based industry consultants Petroleum Finance Company.
International benchmark Brent Blend April crude futures were trading four cents lower at $19.36 on London's International Petroleum Exchange at 1648 GMT.

Exports under the United Nations' oil-for-food deal have crept higher in recent weeks as spot sales over and above original sales contracts have been sanctioned by the U.N. in a effort to make up for a shortfall in revenues.
Baghdad is allowed to sell oil to the value of $1 billion in the 90 days to March and another billion dollars' worth by June 9.
But Iraqi State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) and contract lifters are struggling to find homes for cargoes in the well-supplied crude markets of the United States, Europe and the Far East.
Adding to market concerns was a report on Thursday that OPEC producers kept their foot on the accelerator in February, pumping 130,000 barrels per day (bpd) more crude than the previous month.

Production reached 26.77 million barrels per day in February, over 1.7 million bpd above the official output quota of 25.033 million bpd for the 11-member cartel, a survey by Reuters of OPEC officials, oil companies and analysts found.

"When the market was able to absorb everything thrown at it, it didn't matter. But if prices come off much more then OPEC overproduction will become an issue for the market again," said an OPEC member country official.
Sluggish refinery demand means that oil markets are finding it hard to mop up rising crude supplies.

Annual refinery maintenance is stifling demand at many plants in the United States and Europe, while some poor profit margins for European refineries have forced many to reduce their output, thus cutting back on the crude they need to run.

"There is a general feeling that most nearby requirements are covered both sides of the Atlantic, with upcoming (refinery) maintenance programmes reducing demand. Supplies however are expected to remain ample," said Lawrence Eagles of commodity brokers GNI in a daily report on Thursday.
And when the maintenance season in Europe and the United States in over, Asian refiners will be ready to spruce up their own plants.
"Refinery maintenance has started trimming crude demand in the Atlantic Basin, and will be moving to Asia in the second quarter," said Petroleum Finance Company in their report.
"Net crude import requirements of the three main regions are showing exceptionally large declines in the next three months, at a time when Persian Gulf output is reaching a post Gulf War high."
